concept.name: Shooting star
concept.definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the bottom of the range, a long upper shadow, and little or no lower shadow, appearing after an uptrend. Technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal signal: buyers drove price sharply higher intraperiod but sellers forced it back near the open, showing the rally was rejected; it is a hypothesis that needs confirmation.
concept.intuition: The market shot up during the session but fell back to earth before the close, leaving a long tail that shows buyers could not hold the highs.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: the upper shadow is at least about twice the real body, the lower shadow is minimal, and the body sits near the period's low, after a preceding advance. Its geometry is identical to the inverted hammer; the uptrend context is what makes it a shooting star.
concept.failure_modes: In strong bull trends shooting stars frequently mark only brief pauses before new highs. A close near the high of the next candle negates the pattern entirely.
concept.misconceptions: A shooting star is not confirmed bearish until the next candle closes lower; the pattern alone shows rejection, not a completed reversal. It also cannot exist without a preceding uptrend.
concept.example: After a two-week rally, a stock opens at 90.00, surges to 94.00, and closes at 90.20. Traders flag the shooting star and treat a close below 89.00 the next day as confirmation of a downside reversal.
